questions.q: Why does this lesson say a full simulation is needed, rather than relying only on the individual skills practiced separately in Chapters 1 and 2?
options: Because a real review board demands all those skills simultaneously, under a single clock, rather than one at a time
Because the individual skills from Chapters 1 and 2 are not actually useful on their own
Because full simulations are easier to run than practicing any single skill in isolation
Because review boards never actually combine presenting, defending, and whiteboarding in the same session
questions.explain: The individual skills were taught separately because that's easier to practice, but a real board demands presenting, structuring, defending, handling ambiguity, and recovering from mistakes all at once, under one clock -- which only a full simulation actually rehearses.

questions.q: What specific breadth was the healthcare-consolidation scenario in this lesson deliberately sized to force?
options: A scenario focused entirely on front-end visual design with no backend considerations
Real decisions across data model, integration, security, and phased delivery -- the same breadth a real board probes
A scenario with no integration requirements at all
A purely theoretical scenario with no business constraints
questions.explain: The scenario's external API integration, healthcare data-privacy requirement, staff scale across locations, and phased budget-constrained delivery were chosen specifically to force decisions spanning data, integration, security, and delivery planning.

questions.q: Per this lesson, how can a solo practitioner (with no study partner) still run a meaningful simulation?
options: Simulations are impossible without a real panel, so solo practice should be skipped entirely
By only reading about the scenario silently without ever speaking the design aloud
By designing the solution under a real time limit, recording themselves presenting out loud, and separately answering their own hardest imagined questions out loud as if asked live
By skipping the design phase and jumping straight to memorizing answers
questions.explain: The solo structure still forces the actual verbal and sequencing skills by having the practitioner present out loud and answer self-generated hard questions aloud -- more useful than only rehearsing silently in one's head, even though it feels artificial at first.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a simulation that isn't reviewed afterward is 'just a rehearsal, not a practice cycle'?
options: Because rehearsals and practice cycles are exactly the same thing
Because only a panel of real CTAs can turn a rehearsal into a practice cycle
Because capturing time-budget accuracy, unstated assumptions, mistake recovery, and the hardest questions afterward is what turns the exercise into material that improves the next attempt
Because debriefing is only useful for simulations that went badly
questions.explain: Capturing specific, concrete outcomes from the run -- not just completing it -- is what makes it feed into improvement; the hardest questions from a run are described as the highest-value material for the next simulation, not a sign of failure.

questions.q: How do Lessons 12 and 13 build on this lesson's general simulation, per this lesson's framing?
options: They replace this lesson's scenario and process entirely with an unrelated approach
They reuse the same simulation structure but deliberately load the questioning toward one specific domain each -- security in Lesson 12, integration in Lesson 13
They remove the time-limit element introduced in this lesson
They are only relevant to candidates who already passed a real review board
questions.explain: This lesson's general-purpose version gives a baseline covering a spread of domains; Lessons 12 and 13 reuse the same structure but deliberately concentrate questioning on security and integration respectively, the way a real board sometimes does when a panelist's specialty or an earlier answer invites deeper probing.
